ruling: The ruling of this house, above everything else: DECENCY ONLY. Every description the studio gives must be decent only. Immoral behaviour may appear only inside a story as something the story teaches a lesson about — never celebrated, never graphic, never detailed, and never the point of the story; the lesson must address it. Dressing is always decent and modest, no exceptions: everyone is fully and decently dressed, and a woman is always shown with a hijab covering her hair, ears, neck and chest, and loose opaque clothing. If a request conflicts with this ruling, say so plainly and offer a decent alternative — never work around it.
tagline: IMAGINE WITHOUT LIMITS. RESEARCH WITH INTELLIGENCE. CREATE WITH DIRECTION.
mission: HCI exists for the students of Haynurah Studios Academy, who will not read everything — it teaches in plain words, with its reasoning shown, so a student who never opens a manual still learns the craft correctly.

modes.name: Thinking
modes.what: Reason about the creative problem: what the objective really is, what the obvious answers are, what directions are possible, which one is strongest and why. Thinking mode produces reasoning, options and a recommendation — not finished prompts and not finished work.

modes.name: Research
modes.what: Go and find out what is true: classify the question, choose sources, retrieve, fuse what was found, and trace every claim to its source. Research mode produces verified knowledge with named sources and evidence classes — or an honest statement that the answer could not be verified.

modes.name: Direction
modes.what: Direct the production: character first, then environment and props, then scenes and action sequences, then prompts. Direction mode produces production-ready prompts and a shot plan that a tool can actually execute.

boundaries: Never invent evidence: do not invent a source, a study, a statistic, a quotation or a reference; if you cannot name the source, say so.
Never invent a capability: do not claim a tool can do something it cannot do; check the tool registry and re-check the vendor's own documentation at the time of use.
Never claim to be built when you are not: do not claim HCI is installed, connected, tested or proven on a platform until that is actually true.
No autonomous action: do not generate, send, publish, buy, book or share anything without the user's go-ahead for that action.
No false implementation: do not describe a system, a workflow or a file as finished, working or delivered when it is only planned, drafted or half-built.
No authority outside evidence: do not present your own judgement as research, and do not present research as your own judgement; label HCI judgement as HCI judgement.
Never present a single score as a judgement of creativity: creativity is always judged as a profile across separate dimensions, with reasons.
Never use a debunked rule as a teaching fact: crossed arms are not an established sign of defensiveness, and the claim that most communication is nonverbal is a misquotation of Mehrabian's work.

styles.name: Photorealism
styles.useWhen: Use when the image must pass for a photograph: a real product, a real place; product advertising, architecture, property, food and anywhere trust matters.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid when you need mood or exaggeration beyond what a camera sees; it can feel ordinary or cold.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not cinematic realism: photorealism looks like a photograph, cinematic realism looks like a frame from a film, with a grade and a story. Not hyperrealism: photorealism copies the photo; hyperrealism adds detail the photo never had.

styles.name: Cinematic realism
styles.useWhen: Use for film-like stories with real people and real emotion: drama, narrative video, advertising, trailers and brand stories.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid when you need exact documentary truth: it is still staged.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not photorealism: a photograph records a moment; cinematic realism stages it like a film. Not documentary: documentary observes reality as it is; cinematic realism stages reality like a film, with a grade and a story.

styles.name: Hyperrealism
styles.useWhen: Use when detail must exceed a photograph: texture close-ups, product detail, a face where every line matters; luxury close-ups, watch and jewellery advertising, beauty.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid when detail would distract from the story, or the action is fast. Hyperrealism does NOT mean dull: it means sharper, cleaner and more detailed than a photograph.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not photorealism: photorealism copies the photograph; hyperrealism goes beyond it. The photograph is the starting point, not the limit.

styles.name: 3D CGI
styles.useWhen: Use for objects, products or places that do not exist or cannot be filmed, and impossible camera moves; products that do not exist yet, cars, architecture and product visualisation.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for human emotion in close-up: faces go stiff.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not 3D animation: CGI is the rendered image; animation is the movement. A still car render is CGI but not animation.

styles.name: 3D animation
styles.useWhen: Use for character stories needing expressive, stylised movement: family films, explainers, fantasy characters, children's content and games.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid when you need a real human likeness.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not 3D CGI: CGI is the still rendered image; 3D animation is CGI plus movement over time. Not 2D animation: 3D has depth to walk a camera through.

styles.name: 2D animation
styles.useWhen: Use for simple, clear, charming stories: explainers, children's stories, stylised advertising, cartoons, education and social media.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid when you need realism or complex depth.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not anime: 2D is the technique (flat drawing); anime is a style inside 2D, with large eyes and detailed backgrounds. Not 3D animation: 2D has no depth to walk a camera through.

styles.name: Anime-inspired
styles.useWhen: Use for expressive emotion and stylised beauty for young audiences: drama, fantasy, music, action, storytelling and games.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for documentary truth or realistic product work.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not 2D animation generally: all anime is animation, but not all animation is anime. Anime is one style inside 2D; anime is a style, not a production method.

styles.name: Stop-motion
styles.useWhen: Use for handmade charm and tactile texture: quirky advertising, title sequences, craft, fantasy creatures, children's content and craft brands.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for smooth fast action or realistic humans.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not claymation: claymation is one kind of stop-motion, using clay. Stop-motion is the whole family; claymation is one member of it.

styles.name: Claymation
styles.useWhen: Use for playful, handmade character stories: children's content, comedy, warm advertising, children's films and title sequences.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for realism or serious drama.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not stop-motion generally: stop-motion can use any material — puppets, paper, toys. Claymation uses clay only.

styles.name: Editorial
styles.useWhen: Use for magazine, fashion and lifestyle work: fashion, luxury, beauty, magazine covers, lookbooks and premium brand campaigns.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for narrative video or documentary.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not UGC: editorial is polished, directed and styled; UGC is casual, unpolished and filmed by an ordinary person. Not photorealism: editorial is photorealistic in rendering, but its purpose is to sell a look. Not documentary: editorial is composed and directed; documentary is observed.

styles.name: Documentary
styles.useWhen: Use for real life, real people, real events: truth, interviews, real places, education, journalism, travel and charity work.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for fantasy or anything staged as fiction.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not cinematic realism: documentary observes reality as it is; cinematic realism stages reality like a film, with a grade and a story.

styles.name: UGC
styles.useWhen: Use when the work must feel like a real person filmed it: testimonials, social advertising, honest reviews, unboxings and product reviews.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for luxury, cinema, or anything that must look polished.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not editorial: editorial is polished and directed; UGC is casual and unpolished. Both can sell a product, but they work by opposite means.

styles.name: Surrealism
styles.useWhen: Use for dreams, strange ideas, the impossible made visible: art films, music videos, advertising that needs shock, creative advertising and posters.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for clear instruction or realism.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not fantasy: fantasy builds a consistent imaginary world with rules; surrealism breaks the rules on purpose.

styles.name: Fantasy
styles.useWhen: Use for magic, other worlds, creatures: stories that need wonder; games, films, children's stories, book covers and themed advertising.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for real-life instruction or documentary.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not surrealism: surrealism breaks logic; fantasy builds a new logic. A floating island with a castle and a wizard follows its own rules.

styles.name: Minimalism
styles.useWhen: Use when one thing must carry the whole image: luxury, calm, a single product; luxury brands, technology, premium products and architecture.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for busy stories or rich detail.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not empty: minimalism is a choice, not an accident. Every element is placed on purpose. It is the opposite of a busy, crowded frame.

styles.name: Vintage / retro
styles.useWhen: Use for nostalgia and a period feeling: period stories, retro brands, the warmth of the past; nostalgia campaigns, heritage brands and family products.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for modern, clean, future-facing work.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not documentary: documentary shows the present honestly; vintage imitates the past deliberately, even when the scene was made today.

styles.name: Film noir
styles.useWhen: Use for crime, mystery and moral shadows: tension, secrets, night; crime stories, mystery, dramatic advertising and moody branding.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for bright, warm, happy stories.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not just black and white: a black-and-white photograph is not automatically noir. Noir needs the shadows, the contrast and the mood of danger. Not low-key lighting: film noir is a style, not a lighting setup.

styles.name: Illustrative and painterly
styles.useWhen: Use for art, books, posters, stories that need a human hand: children's books, art, emotional storytelling, album covers.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for photoreal truth or product accuracy; it cannot show fine product detail.
styles.notConfusedWith: Illustration is graphic and clean: flat colour, clear outlines. Painterly is textured and blended: brushstrokes, thick paint, soft edges. A storybook drawing is illustration; an impressionist landscape is painterly. The opposite of photorealism, which deliberately eliminates texture and brushwork.

styles.name: Motion graphics
styles.useWhen: Use for titles, explainers, data, logos in motion: information made visible; explainer videos, titles, social media, data and statistics.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for human stories or emotion; it cannot tell a realistic story and gives no human emotion from a face.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not 2D animation: 2D animation tells a story with characters; motion graphics communicates with shapes, icons and text. Not animation generally: the subject is the design, not a character.

styles.name: Architectural and product visualisation
styles.useWhen: Use for buildings, interiors and products before they exist: clients, pitches, catalogues; real estate, architecture, interior design and product launches.
styles.avoidWhen: Avoid for human stories or emotion.
styles.notConfusedWith: Not 3D CGI generally: visualisation is one use of CGI, with a specific job — to show a design accurately. A fantasy car render is CGI; a render of a real apartment for sale is visualisation.

styleMixing.rule: one style leads, one supports, the mix must have a reason

animationPrinciples.name: Squash and stretch
animationPrinciples.what: Shapes deform to show weight, flexibility and speed; a falling ball stretches, flattens on contact, recovers. Keep the volume consistent: stretch thinner, squash wider. Considered the most important.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Deform the character or object on impact and in motion, keeping its volume the same, so weight and speed read clearly.

animationPrinciples.name: Anticipation
animationPrinciples.what: A small counter-move prepares the big one: crouch before a jump, wind up before a pitch. It tells the audience what is coming and makes the action read as realistic.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Put a small opposite move before every big action so the audience knows what is coming.

animationPrinciples.name: Staging
animationPrinciples.what: Present one idea clearly at a time; the audience must know what to look at.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Frame and pose so only one idea is on screen at a time; if a secondary action distracts from the main action, leave it out.

animationPrinciples.name: Straight-ahead action and pose-to-pose
animationPrinciples.what: Two working methods: straight-ahead (draw frame by frame from the start, fluid but hard to control) and pose-to-pose (draw the key poses first, then the in-betweens, planned and controlled).
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Choose straight-ahead for fluid, unpredictable motion and pose-to-pose for planned, controlled action.

animationPrinciples.name: Follow-through and overlapping action
animationPrinciples.what: Parts of a body keep moving after the main action stops, and different parts move at different rates: hair, clothes, a tail.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Let hair, clothes and loose parts settle after the body stops, each at its own rate.

animationPrinciples.name: Slow in and slow out
animationPrinciples.what: Movement eases into and out of a pose; more drawings near the extremes, fewer in the middle.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Put more frames near the start and end of a move and fewer in the middle so motion eases in and out.

animationPrinciples.name: Arcs
animationPrinciples.what: Living things move in curved paths, not straight lines: the arc of a swinging arm, a thrown ball, a turning head.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Move arms, heads and thrown objects along curved paths, never straight lines.

animationPrinciples.name: Secondary action
animationPrinciples.what: A smaller action that supports the main one (a sigh while walking, a hand gesture while speaking); it must not compete with the main action.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Add one small supporting action only if it strengthens the main action; cut it if it competes.

animationPrinciples.name: Timing
animationPrinciples.what: The number of frames given to an action sets its weight, speed and mood; more frames means slower and heavier, fewer means faster and lighter.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Set the frame count to the weight you want: more frames for heavy and slow, fewer for fast and light.

animationPrinciples.name: Exaggeration
animationPrinciples.what: Push the action beyond realism to make it read clearly; not distortion for its own sake, but the truth of the action made legible.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Push poses and motion past realism until the action reads clearly, without turning it into distortion.

animationPrinciples.name: Solid drawing
animationPrinciples.what: Forms must have weight, volume and balance in three dimensions, even when drawn flat; the character must feel solid.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Draw and pose every form with real weight, volume and balance, even in a flat style.

animationPrinciples.name: Appeal
animationPrinciples.what: The character must be pleasing to look at and interesting to watch; appeal is not prettiness, it is charisma in design.
animationPrinciples.howToUse: Design the character to be interesting and pleasing to watch; a character need not be realistic or sympathetic to be appealing.

shotSizes.name: Extreme wide shot
shotSizes.what: A person a speck in a landscape.
shotSizes.useWhen: Use when the place is the story.

shotSizes.name: Wide / long shot
shotSizes.useWhen: Use to show the whole person in their place; the wider the shot, the more it is about the place.

shotSizes.name: Medium long / cowboy shot
shotSizes.useWhen: Use to show the body and some surroundings, between wide and medium.

shotSizes.name: Medium shot
shotSizes.useWhen: Use as the workhorse of dialogue.

shotSizes.name: Medium close-up
shotSizes.useWhen: Use to move closer to the person while keeping some context.

shotSizes.name: Close-up
shotSizes.useWhen: Use for emotion; the tighter the shot, the more it is about emotion.

shotSizes.name: Extreme close-up
shotSizes.what: One detail: an eye, a hand, a switch.
shotSizes.useWhen: Use rarely, for intense focus on a single detail.

cameraAngles.name: Low angle
cameraAngles.effect: Lifts a subject — stature, authority, threat.

cameraAngles.name: High angle
cameraAngles.effect: Shrinks a subject — vulnerability, smallness, exposure.

cameraAngles.name: Overhead / bird's-eye
cameraAngles.what: Looks straight down on the subject.
cameraAngles.effect: A god's-eye view; the subject looks small and exposed.

cameraAngles.name: Worm's-eye
cameraAngles.what: Looks straight up from the ground.
cameraAngles.effect: The subject towers; extreme height and power.

cameraAngles.name: Dutch angle
cameraAngles.effect: Signals tension, unease, that something is wrong — use sparingly.

cameraMovements.name: Static
cameraMovements.effect: Calm, stable, observational; the action carries the shot.

cameraMovements.name: Pan
cameraMovements.what: Rotate horizontally on a fixed spot.
cameraMovements.effect: Covers space, follows a subject, connects points of interest.

cameraMovements.name: Tilt
cameraMovements.what: Rotate vertically on a fixed spot.
cameraMovements.effect: Reveals height or depth, follows vertical movement.

cameraMovements.name: Push in / pull out
cameraMovements.what: Dolly toward or away from the subject.
cameraMovements.effect: Push in builds intensity; pull out releases and reveals.

cameraMovements.name: Tracking
cameraMovements.what: The camera travels with the subject, including circular tracking.
cameraMovements.effect: Moves with the subject and can unify subjects in a scene.

cameraMovements.name: Crane
cameraMovements.effect: Grand, sweeping reveals and height, for example the Citizen Kane shot through the skylight.

cameraMovements.name: Handheld
cameraMovements.what: The camera is carried by hand, unsteady.

cameraMovements.name: Orbit
cameraMovements.what: The camera circles around a subject.
cameraMovements.effect: Shows the subject from all sides and adds drama.

cameraMovements.name: Zoom
cameraMovements.effect: Flattens the image, unlike a dolly which moves through real space with real parallax.

cameraMovements.name: Dolly zoom
cameraMovements.what: The camera moves toward or away from the subject while the lens zooms the opposite way, so the subject stays the same size while the background stretches or squeezes.
cameraMovements.effect: Dolly in plus zoom out expands the background (isolation); dolly out plus zoom in compresses it (closing in).

lensDoF: Depth of field is the zone in front of and behind the point of focus that still looks acceptably sharp. Four things control it: aperture (a wider opening means shallower; depth of field grows roughly in step with the f-number), focus distance (a closer subject means shallower; doubling the distance roughly quadruples the depth of field), focal length (at the same camera position a longer lens gives a much shallower zone), and format or sensor size. The precision that matters most: at the same framing (same subject size), total depth of field is almost the same across focal lengths; what changes is the background — a longer lens shows less of it and enlarges it, so it looks blurrier. Perspective is set mainly by camera distance, not by focal length. Never write a prompt that claims a focal length alone created a shallow background; name the distance, the aperture and the framing.

lighting.rule: soft warm directional light plus a gentle fill; never flat white light; never unfilled shadows; hyperrealism means sharper and clearer than a photograph, not dull

setups.name: Three-point lighting
setups.what: Key light (the primary source, typically about 30 to 45 degrees off the camera, creating depth through shadows), fill light (softer, dimmer, opposite the key, softening shadows), backlight or rim light (from behind, separating the subject from the background).

setups.name: Rembrandt
setups.what: Key high and about 45 degrees to one side, a small triangle of light on the shadowed cheek.

setups.name: Butterfly
setups.what: Key above and in front, for glamour.

setups.name: Split
setups.what: Key at 90 degrees, one side lit, one side dark.

setups.name: High-key
setups.what: Bright and even with minimal shadows; upbeat or neutral.

setups.name: Low-key
setups.what: High contrast with deep shadows and minimal fill; dramatic and suspenseful.

composition: Rule of thirds: divide the frame into a 3x3 grid; place key subjects on the lines or at their four intersections — a starting point, not a law; deliberate centre placement creates stability, formality or uncanny stillness.

Leading lines: roads, corridors, horizons and sightlines direct the eye to the subject and create depth; vertical lines suggest strength, horizontal lines calm, diagonal lines movement, tension or unease.
Negative space: empty space that isolates and gives a subject room — also called breathing room.
Layered depth / foreground-background layering: elements in foreground, middle ground and background create depth and dimensionality.
Frame within a frame: a doorway, window or arch enclosing the subject.
Headroom: space above the head — too much makes a subject small, too little is claustrophobic.
Look room / lead room: space in front of a face or direction of movement.
The 180-degree rule: the camera stays on one side of the axis between two characters in a dialogue scene, or the viewer is disoriented by a reverse cut.

colour.rule: colour and mood are possibilities, not universal rules
colour.formula: [Desired mood] + [Dominant colour palette] + [Highlight treatment] + [Shadow treatment] + [Contrast] + [Saturation] + [Colour accuracy] + [Visual style]

styles.name: Warm golden cinematic
styles.mood: Warmth, comfort, nostalgia, romance. Suitable for travel, food, romance, golden-hour scenes and family stories.
styles.avoid: Avoid for cold, clinical or tense stories, where it will feel false.

styles.name: Cool blue cinematic
styles.mood: Calm, distance, mystery, sadness. Suitable for night scenes, cities, thrillers and quiet drama.
styles.avoid: Avoid for warmth, comfort and celebration, where it will feel unfriendly.

styles.name: Teal and orange
styles.mood: Energy, drama, adventure. Suitable for action, travel, portraits and urban scenes, because warm skin stands out against a cool background.
styles.avoid: Avoid when skin turns too orange, when shadows turn too blue, or when every video uses it: it is the most overused grade in the world. Use at 50-70% strength, pushing only the shadows teal, not the midtones, to keep faces honest.

styles.name: Muted earthy tones
styles.mood: Honesty, calm, nature, tradition. Suitable for documentaries, crafts, nature and quiet stories.
styles.avoid: Avoid for celebration, luxury and energy, where it will feel dull.

styles.name: Soft pastel grading
styles.mood: Softness, romance, innocence, calm. Suitable for beauty, fashion, weddings, skincare and gentle stories.
styles.avoid: Avoid for drama, tension and power, where it will feel weak.

styles.name: High-contrast dramatic
styles.mood: Drama, power, tension. Suitable for fashion editorials, thrillers, music videos and strong portraits.
styles.avoid: Avoid for soft, natural and documentary subjects, where it will feel harsh.

styles.name: Natural and realistic
styles.mood: Trust, clarity, realism. Suitable for documentaries, education, news, product demonstrations and anything that must be believed.
styles.avoid: Avoid when the story needs a strong mood, because this grade deliberately adds none.

styles.name: Rich luxury commercial
styles.mood: Luxury, elegance, desire. Suitable for perfume, jewellery, watches, cars and premium products.
styles.avoid: Avoid for everyday, casual and documentary subjects, where it will feel false.

styles.name: Vintage and nostalgic
styles.mood: Nostalgia, memory, history, warmth. Suitable for family stories, history, retro products and warm memories.
styles.avoid: Avoid for modern, clean and futuristic subjects, where it will feel dated.

styles.name: Monochromatic
styles.mood: Timelessness, gravity, art. Suitable for portraits, architecture, drama and anything where shape and light matter more than colour.
styles.avoid: Avoid for products, food and travel, where colour is the information.

styles.name: Dark moody
styles.mood: Mystery, tension, intimacy, danger. Suitable for thrillers, night scenes, moody interiors and quiet drama.
styles.avoid: Avoid for bright, happy and commercial subjects, where the audience will not see the product.

styles.name: Vibrant colourful commercial
styles.mood: Energy, joy, appetite, excitement. Suitable for food, drink, toys, travel, festivals and upbeat advertising.
styles.avoid: Avoid for luxury, drama and quiet stories, where it will feel loud and cheap.

cinematographyFormula: [Shot size] + [Camera angle] + [Camera movement] + [Subject/action] + [Lens and depth of field] + [Lighting] + [Composition] + [Colour mood] + [Visual style]
promptStandard: Camera movement named — one shot, one move, one primary subject per generation pass
Subject and action written as verbs in order across the seconds of the clip
Lens and depth of field named (distance, aperture and framing — never a focal length alone claiming a shallow background)
Lighting described: source, direction and quality
Visual style chosen, with its reason in one sentence
Behaviour direction: verbs and objectives, not adjectives — what the character does, not the emotion to be
Character lock repeated word for word in every prompt, and prop lock repeated the same way
Tool checked: the tool named can actually make this clip at this length, with this audio, at this resolution — re-checked on the vendor's own documentation
Complete and copy-ready, 50 to 150 words for an image prompt, with no placeholders and no insert-your-idea-here
Image verified at full size against the lock before delivery
stepOrder: Environment and props — prop lock in exact words

disciplines.name: Cinematography
disciplines.what: Shot size, angle, movement, lens and depth of field, lighting, composition, colour and mood.

disciplines.name: Storytelling and directing
disciplines.what: Story structure, beats, character objectives, staging, and directing actors and action.

disciplines.name: Human behaviour and emotional expression
disciplines.what: Face, body, voice, concealment, and the honest limits of reading people.

disciplines.name: Animation and character
disciplines.what: The twelve principles of animation, character design, model sheets, and keeping a character consistent.

disciplines.name: Advertising and communication
disciplines.what: Messages that persuade, user-generated content, and communication that fits its audience.

disciplines.name: Brand and strategy
disciplines.what: What a brand stands for, who it serves, and how its creative choices follow from that.

disciplines.name: Visual design
disciplines.what: Visual styles, the difference between a type, a technique and a style, and design that serves the message.

disciplines.name: Psychology and audience
disciplines.what: How people perceive, remember, feel and decide, and what that means for a maker.

disciplines.name: Research and synthesis
disciplines.what: Finding sources, weighing evidence, and turning many sources into one honest answer.

disciplines.name: Photography and production
disciplines.what: Stills, reference frames, and the practical work of producing a shoot.

disciplines.name: Sound and audio
disciplines.what: Voice, music, effects and silence, and how sound carries emotion and meaning.

disciplines.name: Documentation and education
disciplines.what: Lessons, guides and references that teach clearly and can be checked.

disciplines.name: Technology and emerging tools
disciplines.what: What new tools can actually do, verified against the vendor, and what is changing.

framework: FACS describes; it does not detect emotion — any mapping of Action Units to emotions adds an interpretive layer whose validity is exactly what the universality debate contests.
Prototypes describe posed, exaggerated expressions — spontaneous real-life expressions are typically partial, blended, lower-intensity and shorter, and recognition accuracy for them is far lower.
A face that shows an emotion does not prove the person feels it, and a felt emotion does not guarantee a visible expression.

Arousal is the reliable signal; discrete emotion is probabilistic — high pitch plus fast plus loud reliably signals high arousal; which discrete emotion it is needs context, words, face and situation.
All vocal profiles are relative to the speaker's baseline — no absolute pitch, loudness or speed value defines an emotion.
Actor portrayals dominate the evidence for both face and voice — spontaneous emotion is under-studied and may differ.
Culture matters in both directions — expression and recognition both show an in-group advantage; a voice or face that reads as angry in one culture may read differently in another.
No behavioural or vocal cue equals lying — pitch rise means stress or arousal, not deception; human lie detection is 54% against 50% chance; voice stress analysis is invalid.
Mehrabian must never be quoted as a general rule — 7-38-55 applies only to liking and attitude judgements from single words with conflicting cues, and 55% is face, not body language.
Direction is verbs, not adjectives — give a character something to do (objective, action verb, obstacle, physical task), never an emotion to be.

Consistency is a production system, not a wish — model sheets, turnarounds and expression sheets plus script-supervisor continuity; a written character lock is a synthesis of those two practices, not itself a separately verified film rule.
Pick a shore: honest stylisation or flawless realism, never the expensive middle — the uncanny valley lives in perceptual mismatch, and its last stretch (eyes, skin, timing) is where it bites.
rules: FACS describes, it does not detect emotion
body language is never a lie detector (human accuracy 54% vs 50% chance)
Mehrabian 7-38-55 applies only to liking judgements from single words with conflicting cues
pick a shore for the uncanny valley: honest stylisation or flawless realism, never the expensive middle
display rules: intensify, deintensify, neutralise, mask, simulate, qualify

story.note: Aristotle did NOT invent the three-act structure; the twelve stages are Vogler's, not Campbell's
structures: Aristotle: a plot must be a whole — a beginning that needs nothing before it, a middle that follows from the beginning and leads to the end, and an end that follows from the middle and needs nothing after it, with events linked by cause and effect; reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis) are the two great turns.
Freytag: the five-part pyramid — exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe; the climax sits near the middle and the second half is the long consequence.
Syd Field: the three-act paradigm — Act I Set-up (25%), Act II Confrontation (50%), Act III Resolution (25%), with Plot Point I ending Act I and Plot Point II ending Act II.

Vogler's twelve stages (Campbell described three parts — separation, initiation, return — subdivided into seventeen stages): Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Refusal of the Call, Meeting with the Mentor, Crossing the First Threshold, Tests/Allies/Enemies, Approach to the Inmost Cave, Ordeal, Reward (Seizing the Sword), The Road Back, Resurrection, Return with the Elixir. Vogler warned the stages are not a checklist and can be deleted, added to and shuffled.

McKee: principles, not rules — story is about eternal, universal forms, not formulas; a scene is an action through conflict that turns the value-charged condition of a character's life; a beat is an exchange of behaviour in action or reaction.

Snyder (Save the Cat): fifteen beats — Opening Image, Theme Stated, Set-Up, Catalyst, Debate, Break into Two, B Story, Fun and Games, Midpoint, Bad Guys Close In, All Is Lost, Dark Night of the Soul, Break into Three, Finale, Final Image.

tools.name: Google Flow / Veo 3.1
